name: Urban wear

card.summary: Hip-hop-rooted streetwear style (logos, sneakers, hoodies, oversized fits) used to build a current, confident look.
card.note: A fashion category; fit and styling determine how it looks.

quick.overview:
Urban wear is the clothing category that grew out of hip-hop and street culture: sneakers, graphic tees, hoodies, branded outerwear and workwear-influenced pieces.

For looks, it is a style framework: people choose it to look current, relaxed and expressive, often built around sneakers and fit. It is usually discussed alongside streetwear and 'hypebeast' culture.
quick.how: People assemble outfits from tees, hoodies, jackets and sneakers from streetwear labels, sometimes through limited releases and resale.
quick.risks: No health risks. Limited releases and resale can make items expensive, and the style has drawn cultural-appropriation criticism.

lead: Urban wear is a clothing category rooted in hip-hop culture, mainly among African American communities in New York from the late 1970s and early 1980s, with sneakers tied to the style early on.[1] Dapper Dan's Harlem boutique (1982) combined luxury logos with custom design, and Shawn Stüssy's printed T-shirts on the West Coast shaped streetwear's focus on tees and exclusivity.[1]

In the 1990s, record labels sold branded merchandise and artists launched labels such as Phat Farm, Sean John and Rocawear.[1] By the 2010s Supreme, Stüssy and BAPE were highly coveted and collaborations with luxury houses followed.[1]
As an appearance approach, it is a way to dress in a recognisable contemporary style; the term 'hypebeast' emerged in the mid-2000s for people who buy streetwear to follow trends.[1]

chain: Choose streetwear staples (sneakers, hoodies, tees, outerwear)
Build outfits in a current, recognisable style
angle.text: Clothing choice changes appearance directly. Urban wear is one style direction, relying heavily on sneakers, fit and branding.

paras: Sneaker collecting became established in the late 1980s, partly driven by Air Jordans, and the Air Force 1 gained prominence in hip-hop.[1] Skateboarding and gangsta rap were major influences by the mid-1990s, and Jil Sander and Adidas collaborated in 1998.[1]
Complex named Stüssy, Supreme and BAPE top streetwear brands in 2011, and Virgil Abloh's work helped popularise streetwear globally.[1]
Exclusivity relies on limited releases and resale markets, and streetwear's move into luxury fashion has drawn cultural appropriation criticism.[1]

timeline.event: Dapper Dan opens his Harlem boutique.[1]
